papers.title: Himalayan Tartary Buckwheat Sprout Powder, Perceived Cognitive Abilities, and Objective Processing Speed: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial
papers.abstract: Subjective cognitive difficulties are common in midlife and later life, and flavonoid-rich foods may support everyday cognitive function. Tartary buckwheat (Fagopyrum tataricum) sprouts are rich in rutin and other flavonoids, but their cognitive effects have not been tested in humans. In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, US adults with self-reported cognitive difficulties received 18 g per day of Himalayan Tartary buckwheat (HTB) sprout powder or matched placebo for 12 weeks. Of 848 randomized participants, 662 were analyzed. While the rate of change in the primary outcome, PROMIS Cognitive Function, did not differ between arms (contrast = 0.03, 95% CI -0.07 to 0.13; p = .59),PROMIS Cognitive Abilities improved nominally faster with HTB (contrast = 0.12, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.24; p = .046), but not after Bonferroni adjustment. Among participants with final-week data (n = 296), more HTB than placebo participants achieved a meaningful ([≥]0.5 SD) improvement in Cognitive Abilities (68.7% vs 52.5%; RR = 1.32, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.59; p = .003). Fatigue, sleep-related impairment and depressive symptoms did not differ between arms. In exploratory computerized testing (n = 512), HTB participants had faster reaction times on the Flanker and Stroop tasks, without loss of accuracy. Exploratory epigenetic analyses (n = 34) identified hypothesis-generating signals in epigenetic age and immune-cell composition, none surviving multiple-testing correction. Side-effect rates were similar between arms. HTB sprout powder did not improve the primary outcome, but findings for perceived cognitive abilities and processing speed warrant confirmation in adequately powered trials. Trial registration: NCT07245784.

papers.title: False-Positive Calls of Reimplemented Published Analyses for Covert Command-Following on Electroencephalograms Recorded Without Study Commands
papers.abstract: Objective: To measure how often published electroencephalographic analyses for covert command-following call patients positive without commands, and their detection of genuine responses. Methods: This cross-sectional study applied 11 reimplemented published analyses to electroencephalograms without commands: 974 clinical electroencephalography patients and, with rules fixed, 730 new patients; 38 with prolonged disorders of consciousness; and 544 comatose patients after cardiac arrest. Outcomes: false calls (share called positive) against a 5% benchmark, and genuine-response detection. Results: Three of 10 command-following analyses called significantly more than 5% of clinical electroencephalography patients positive, replicated in new patients: Goldfine 2011, a spectral test, 23.3% (95% CI, 20.2%-26.6%), above its stated 5%; du Bois 2026, a criterion for entry to brain-computer interface training, 22.2% (95% CI, 19.2%-25.5%); and Guger 2018, a P300 accuracy threshold, 13.8% (95% CI, 11.5%-16.3%), near its approximate 12% chance rate (24.5% over 2 runs). The other 7 called 0.0% to 6.9%. After cardiac arrest: 11.5% to 27.3%. All 3 detected genuine responses. Identified contributors: a variance ignoring within-command dependence (Goldfine 2011), selection over configurations and times (du Bois 2026) and a permissive threshold (Guger 2018). Goldfine 2011's command-level correction, fixed before testing, called 0.8% of new patients and 2.4% after arrest, detecting 93.4% of stroke imagery-versus-rest sessions but few between imagery types. Interpretation: Reimplemented published analyses called up to 27% of patients positive without commands, more with repeated runs. A positive result needs its complete call rule's false-call rate and detection at that rate; imagery-versus-rest detection may reflect task engagement, not imagery. papers.title: Smaller Cortical Responses to Balance Perturbations in Parkinson's Disease with Freezing of Gait
papers.abstract: Freezing of gait (FoG) is among the most disabling symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD) and is associated with balance impairment and increased falls risk, yet remains challenging to understand due to its episodic and context-dependent nature. Altered supplementary motor area (SMA) function at rest and before self-initiated movements has been implicated in FoG; however, whether this extends to functionally relevant balance behavior is unknown. A loss of balance in response to support surface translations during standing elicits a perturbation-evoked N1 potential, an error assessment signal linked to SMA activity. We therefore predicted that people with FoG would have smaller and later N1 responses than people with PD without FoG and older adults. We recorded electroencephalography (EEG) during backward support-surface translations in 29 people with PD (71 {+/-} 7 years), including 13 people with a history of FoG (FoG+) and 16 people without FoG (FoG-), and 26 older adults (OA; 67 {+/-} 6 years). N1 amplitude and latency were quantified at a central midline electrode and defined as the largest negative peak 100-300 ms post-perturbation. N1 responses were similar between OA and FoG- ({Delta} = 4.0 {micro}V and 2.8 ms, respectively). In contrast, FoG+ had smaller N1 amplitudes than FoG- ({Delta} = 18.1 {micro}V, p = 0.001) and OA ({Delta} = 14.1 {micro}V, p = 0.003), and both differences persisted after adjusting for age. FoG+ also had later N1 latencies than OA ({Delta} = 26.5 ms, p = 0.029), with a similar but non-significant difference versus FoG- ({Delta} = 23.6 ms, p = 0.091); after adjusting for age, these latency differences were not retained. These findings suggest that perturbation-evoked cortical activity is altered in FoG, potentially reflecting altered SMA function, and may provide a functionally relevant marker of FoG susceptibility.

papers.title: First-trimester nocturnal cardiorespiratory coupling during home sleep testing and later pregnancy complications: a secondary analysis of the nuMoM2b cohort
papers.abstract: We tested whether direction-specific nocturnal cardiorespiratory coupling (CRC) in the first trimester differed in pregnancies that later developed obstetric complications. The analysis included 2504 nulliparous women from the nuMoM2b cohort with valid level 3 home sleep recordings at 6-13 weeks' gestation. Bidirectional CRC between RR intervals and abdominal respiratory effort was quantified using bivariate phase-rectified signal averaging in consecutive 5-min segments. Coupling strength, local transition dynamics, and waveform irregularity were summarized by nightly mean and standard deviation. Associations with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM; n = 111), preeclampsia (n = 149), preterm birth (n = 192), and fetal macrosomia (n = 186) were examined using proportional-odds models with CRC feature quintile as the ordered outcome. Models included all four complications simultaneously and adjusted for maternal age, pre-pregnancy body mass index, race and ethnicity, gestational age at recording, relevant medical and family history, medication use, and apnea-hypopnea index >5 events/h. Holm correction was applied across outcomes. GDM was associated with lower respiration-to-heart rate coupling strength (cumulative odds ratio, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.31-0.64; P < 0.001) and shallower slope at the anchor point (0.63; 0.45-0.89; P = 0.03). Fetal macrosomia was associated with lower within-night variability in heart rate-to-respiration waveform irregularity (0.59; 0.45-0.77; P < 0.001). No associations with preeclampsia or preterm birth remained significant after correction. Direction-specific differences in nocturnal CRC were detectable in the first trimester in pregnancies that later developed GDM or resulted in fetal macrosomia.
authors: van der Hout-van der Jagt, M. B.
